bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding the Cybersecurity Salary Landscape

When you are looking at a cybersecurity salary, the first question is whether you are covered by an award or the National Minimum Wage. From 1 July 2026, the National Minimum Wage is $26.44 per hour, or $1,004.90 per week for a 38-hour week, as set by the Fair Work Ombudsman. Casual employees get $33.05 per hour including the 25% casual loading. But many cybersecurity roles fall under the Professional Employees Award 2020, which sets higher minimums.

### Converting Hourly to Annual Pay

The standard formula is: hourly rate × hours per week × 52. We assume a 38-hour week unless stated otherwise. For example, the National Minimum Wage of $26.44 gives $26.44 × 38 × 52 = $52,245.44 per year. But the award minimum for a graduate cybersecurity professional with a three-year degree is $33.71 per hour, which works out to $33.71 × 38 × 52 = $66,825 annually. That is the Level 1 Graduate professional — pay point 1.1 rate from the Professional Employees Award, confirmed by the analysis of ATO and Fair Work data.

### Award Minimums vs Market Rates

The award minimums are just the floor. According to the Australian Taxation Office’s 2023–24 tax returns, the median salary or wages for a cyber security analyst was $99,733, for a cyber security engineer $133,128, and for a cyber security architect $180,327. Jobs and Skills Australia puts median full-time earnings for ICT Security Specialists at $2,461 per week, or about $127,972 annually. These figures are well above the award minimums. The award applies only where the employer is principally in the IT, telecommunications, or quality auditing industry. A cybersecurity analyst working at a bank, hospital, or government department is not covered by that award and would instead rely on the National Minimum Wage or an enterprise agreement.

### Fortnightly and Take-Home Pay

A fortnight is simply the weekly amount multiplied by two. On the National Minimum Wage of $1,004.90 per week, a full-time employee takes home about $1,842 per fortnight after 2026–27 tax and the Medicare levy (assuming no HECS-HELP and private hospital cover). A cybersecurity analyst on the median $99,733 per year earns about $1,918 per week, or $3,836 per fortnight, with an estimated take-home of $2,973 per fortnight. The [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) page can help you estimate your own net income.

### Casual Loading and Superannuation

If you work as a casual, you receive a 25% loading on top of the minimum hourly rate. For the National Minimum Wage, that is $33.05 per hour. For the award graduate rate, it is $42.14 per hour. Superannuation is paid on top of your ordinary earnings at 12% (the super guarantee rate for 2026–27), up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830. That means on a $66,825 award salary, your employer contributes an extra $8,019 to your super fund. On a $99,733 analyst salary, the super contribution would be $11,968. See [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) for more details.

### Key Distinctions

- **National Minimum Wage**: $26.44/hr, $1,004.90/week, casual $33.05/hr.
- **Professional Employees Award (IT stream)**: Graduate minimum $33.71/hr, $66,825/yr; experienced Level 2 $39.77/hr, $78,836/yr.
- **Market median (ATO)**: Cyber security analyst $99,733; engineer $133,128; architect $180,327.
- **Casual loading**: 25% on top of the minimum hourly rate.
- **Super**: 12% on ordinary earnings, paid on top, capped at $270,830.

Always check whether an award covers your role. If it does, the award rate is your legal minimum. If not, the National Minimum Wage applies. Use [the timesheet](/) to convert your hourly rate to annual, fortnightly, and weekly figures, and see the [pay guides](/blog) for the latest award rates.
